## Overview

Use a regression forest to predict a continuous response from numeric and
categorical predictors. We simulate a known signal, fit on 80 observations, and
evaluate predictions on 20 held-out observations.

## Prerequisites

Follow [Get Started](get-started.html) to install RLT, then load the package:

```{r load-package}
library(RLT)
```

## Data

The first five predictors are numeric and the last five are factors. Factor
columns tell RLT to use categorical splits. The numeric response combines
predictors 2 through 6, an additional effect for categories 1 and 2 of predictor
6, and independent Gaussian noise.

```{r data-prep}
set.seed(1)

trainn <- 80
testn  <- 20
n <- trainn + testn
p <- 10

# Continuous + categorical predictors (last half as factors)
X1 <- matrix(rnorm(n * (p/2)), n, p/2)
X2 <- matrix(as.integer(runif(n * (p/2)) * 3), n, p/2)  # integers 0,1,2

X_numeric <- data.frame(X1, X2)

# Continuous outcome with a simple signal + noise
y <- 1 + rowSums(X_numeric[, 2:6]) + 2 * (X_numeric[, p/2 + 1] %in% c(1, 2)) + rnorm(n)

X <- X_numeric
X[, (p/2 + 1):p] <- lapply(X[, (p/2 + 1):p], as.factor)

# Train / test split
trainX <- X[1:trainn, ]
trainY <- y[1:trainn]
testX  <- X[(trainn + 1):(trainn + testn), ]
testY  <- y[(trainn + 1):(trainn + testn)]
```

## Fit

We use 200 trees and sample half of the predictors as split candidates at each
node with `mtry = p/2`. Setting `nsplit = 0` searches all available cutpoints for
numeric candidates. The explicit `seed` controls fitting randomness; see
[Random Seed and Reproducibility](feature-seed.html) for the distinction from
`set.seed()` used for data generation above.

```{r fit-model}
fit <- RLT(
  trainX, trainY, model = "regression",
  ntrees = 200, mtry = p/2, nsplit = 0,
  seed = 1, ncores = 1, verbose = FALSE
)
```

## Predict

```{r predict}
pred <- predict(fit, testX)
head(data.frame(Observed = testY, Predicted = pred$Prediction))
```

`pred$Prediction` contains one numeric prediction per held-out row. These values
estimate the conditional mean response at the supplied predictor values.

## Evaluate

The fitted object's `Prediction` component contains out-of-bag (OOB)
predictions. Each training observation is predicted using only trees whose
resample omitted it. The test predictions use the fitted forest on observations
reserved before fitting.

```{r evaluate}
list(
  OOB_MSE = round(mean((fit$Prediction - trainY)^2), 4),
  Test_MSE = round(mean((pred$Prediction - testY)^2), 4)
)
```

Both mean squared errors measure prediction error, with smaller values
indicating more accurate predictions. OOB MSE uses the training observations
without including them in the corresponding trees; test MSE uses the 20
held-out observations. Their difference reflects the different evaluation
samples and trees used, and the test estimate is noisy with only 20 observations.

## Inspect

```{r inspect}
print(fit)
```

The printed summary records the forest settings and OOB error. To assess which
predictors the forest relies on, continue to
[Variable Importance](variable-importance.html).
